```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
# This page shows its code.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
themes <- unique(unlist(purrr::map(cfg$target_groups, "theme")))
use_github <- !is.null(cfg$submissions$repos$registry)
use_bucket <- !isFALSE(cfg$submissions$use_bucket)
horizons <- range(variables$max_horizon)
```

## Overview: How to submit a forecast

We provide an overview of the steps for submitting with the details below:

1)  Explore the [data](targets.qmd#sec-targets) (e.g., targets) and build your forecast model.
2)  Register and describe your model `r if (use_github) "in the challenge-model.yaml file in your public git repository (described below), or" else "at"` <`r settings$registration_form_url`>. You are not required to register if your forecast submission uses the word "example" in your model_id. Any forecasts with "example" in the model_id will not be used in forecast evaluation analyses. Use `` `r cfg$project_id` `` as the challenge for which you are registering.
3)  Generate a forecast!
4)  Write the forecast output to a file that follows our standardized format (described below).
5)  Submit your forecast `r if (use_github) "by committing the file to your public git repository "`(described below).
6)  Watch your forecast be evaluated as new data are collected.

## Generating a forecast

### All forecasting approaches are welcome

We encourage you to use any modeling approach to predict the future conditions at any of the sites and variables.

### Must include uncertainty

Forecasts require you to assess the confidence in your prediction of the future.
You can represent your confidence (i.e., uncertainty in the forecast) using a distribution or numerically using an ensemble (or sample) of predictions.

### Any model drivers/covariates/features are welcome

You can use any data as model inputs (including all target data available to date).
You may want to use the updated target data to re-train a model or for use in data assimilation.
As a genuine forecasting challenge, you will need forecasted drivers if your model uses drivers as inputs.

{{< include _content/instructions-drivers.qmd >}}

### Forecasts can be for a range of horizons

How far ahead you can forecast depends on the variable: the longest horizon is between `r horizons[1]` and `r horizons[2]` days.
See the [variable tables](targets.qmd#sec-targets) for the horizon associated with each variable.

### Forecasts can be submitted every day

Since forecasts can be submitted every day, automation is essential.

{{< include _content/instructions-automation.qmd >}}

## You can forecast at any of the sites

If you are just getting started, we recommend a set of [focal sites](targets.qmd#sec-starting-sites) for each of the `r length(cfg$target_groups)` themes.
You are also welcome to submit forecasts to all or a subset of the sites.
More information about the sites can be found in the [site metadata](`r links$sites`).

## Forecast file format

The file is a CSV format with the following columns:

-   `project_id` (optional): a label for the challenge a row is for. Leave it out, or use `` `r cfg$project_id` ``, for rows that belong in this challenge. Rows labelled for another challenge are not stored here.

-   `model_id`: the short name of the model defined as the model_id in your registration.
    The model_id should have no spaces.
    `model_id` should reflect a method to forecast one or a set of target variables and must be unique to the `` `r cfg$project_id` `` challenge.

-   `datetime`: forecast timestamp.
    Format `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` with UTC as the time zone.
    Forecasts submitted with a `%Y-%m-%d` format will be converted to a full datetime assuming UTC mid-night.

-   `reference_datetime`: The start of the forecast; this should be 0 times steps in the future.
    A file may hold more than one reference datetime (for example to submit past forecasts), but for each model, reference datetime, variable and duration only the first forecast submitted is kept.
    Format is `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` with UTC as the time zone.
    Forecasts submitted with a `%Y-%m-%d` format will be converted to a full datetime assuming UTC mid-night.

-   `duration`: the time-step of the forecast, e.g. `P1D` for a daily forecast and `P1W` for a weekly forecast.
    This value should match the duration of the target variable you are forecasting.
    Formatted as [ISO 8601 duration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Durations)

-   `site_id`: code for the site.

-   `family` name of the probability distribution that is described by the parameter values in the parameter column (see list below for accepted distribution).
    An ensemble forecast as a family of `ensemble`.
    See note below about family.

-   `parameter` the parameters for the distribution (see note below about the parameter column) or the number of the ensemble members.
    For example, the parameters for a normal distribution are called `mu` and `sigma`.

-   `variable`: standardized variable name.
    It must match the variable name in the target file.

-   `prediction`: forecasted value for the parameter in the parameter column

## Representing uncertainty

Uncertainty is represented through the family-parameter columns in the file that you submit.

#### Parameteric forecast

For a parametric forecast with a normal distribution, the `family` column would have the word `normal` to designate a normal distribution, and the parameter column must have values of `mu` and `sigma` for each forecasted variable, site_id, depth, and time combination.

Parameteric forecasts for binary variables should use `bernoulli` as the family and `prob` as the parameter.

The following names and parameterization of the distribution are currently supported (family: parameters):

-   `lognormal`: `mu`, `sigma`
-   `normal`: `mu`,`sigma`
-   `bernoulli`: `prob`
-   `beta`: `shape1`, `shape2`
-   `uniform`: `min`, `max`
-   `gamma`: `shape`, `rate`
-   `logistic`: `location`, `scale`
-   `exponential`: `rate`
-   `poisson`: `lambda`

If you are submitting a forecast that is not in the supported list, we recommend using the ensemble format and sampling from your distribution to generate a set of ensemble members that represents your forecast distribution.

#### Ensemble (or sample) forecast

Ensemble (or sample) forecasts use the `family` value of `ensemble` and the `parameter` values are the ensemble index.

When forecasts using the ensemble family are scored, we assume that the ensemble is a set of equally likely realizations sampled from a distribution comparable to that of the observations (i.e., no broad adjustments are required to make the ensemble more consistent with observations).
This is referred to as a "perfect ensemble" by Bröcker and Smith (2007).
Ensemble (or sample) forecasts are transformed to a probability distribution function (e.g., dressed) using the default methods in the `scoringRules` R package (empirical version of the quantile decomposition for the `crps`).

{{< include _content/instructions-examples.qmd >}}

## Submission process

### File name

Save your forecast as a CSV file (compressed files with the csv.gz extension are also accepted).

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
if (use_github) {
  cat("A forecast committed to a git repository can have any file name: we identify it by the model_id and reference_datetime columns inside it, so one file can hold several variables and be used for several challenges.\n\n")
}
if (use_bucket) {
  cat(if (use_github) "A forecast uploaded to the submissions bucket is named" else "Name the file",
      " with the convention `theme_name-year-month-day-model_id.csv`.\n\n",
      "The `theme_name` options are: ", toString(themes), ". The year, month, and day are the year, month, and day the reference_datetime (horizon = 0). For example, if a forecast starts today and tomorrow is the first forecasted day, horizon = 0 would be today and used in the file name.\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

`model_id` is the id for the model name that you specified in the model registration (model_id has no spaces in it).

### `r if (use_github) "Submitting a forecast" else "Uploading forecast"`

`r if (use_github) "New forecast files can be added to your git repository at any time." else "Individual forecast files can be uploaded at any time."`
The csv file can only contain one unique `model_id`. One file can hold several variables, and the same file can be used for several challenges: each keeps only the rows with its own variables, durations and sites.

{{< include _content/instructions-submit.qmd >}}

### When is my forecast shown?

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
settle <- settings$settle_days
if (isTRUE(settle == 0)) {
  cat("A forecast is shown on the \"latest forecast\" views at the next dashboard update after it is read.\n")
} else {
  cat("The \"latest forecast\" on the Overview and the forecast explorer is the newest forecast whose reference date ",
      "is at least ", settle, " day", if (settle != 1) "s", " old, so that most teams have submitted. A forecast for reference date ",
      "D is therefore shown at the dashboard update on day D+", settle, ". Commit (or upload) it by the **end of day D",
      if (settle > 1) paste0("+", settle - 1), " (UTC)**. ",
      "The challenge updates once a day, but GitHub starts scheduled runs at varying times, sometimes hours late, ",
      "so the deadline is a date, not a time of day. A forecast that misses it is still read and scored; ",
      "it just is not the one shown on those views.\n", sep = "")
}
```

## Post-submission

### Processing

After submission, our servers will process each new file by converting it to a [parquet format](`r links$forecasts`) on our public s3 storage.
A `pub_datetime` column will be added that denotes when a forecast was submitted.
[Summaries](`r links$summaries`) are generated of the forecasts provide descriptive statistics of the forecast.

### Evaluation

All forecasts are scored daily using new data until the full horizon of the forecast has been scored.
Forecasts are scored using the `crps` function in the [`scoringRules`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/scoringRules/index.html) R package.
More information about the scoring metric can be found [here](`r links$docs`).

### Comparison

Forecast performance can be compared to the performance of baseline models.
We are automatically submitting the following baseline models:

```{r baselines, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# From the `baselines` entries in the challenge configuration.
method_text <- c(
  climatology = paste("the normal distribution (mean and standard deviation) of that",
                      "day-of-year in the historical observations"),
  weekly_climatology = paste("the mean and standard deviation of that ISO week in the",
                             "historical observations"),
  persistence_rw = paste("a random walk model that assumes no change in the mean behavior,",
                         "initialized using the most recent observation"),
  mean = "the historical mean of the data"
)
baselines <- purrr::imap(cfg$target_groups, function(g, group) {
  purrr::map(g$baselines, function(b) {
    tibble::tibble(model_id = b$model_id, method = b$method, group = group)
  })
}) |>
  purrr::list_flatten() |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  dplyr::summarise(groups = toString(unique(group)), .by = c(model_id, method))
cat(paste0("-   `", baselines$model_id, "`: ", method_text[baselines$method],
           " (", baselines$groups, ")"), sep = "\n")
```

Our [leaderboard](leaderboard.qmd) and [forecast explorer](forecasts.qmd) page includes evaluations of all submitted models.

Our [data](data.qmd) page provides information and code for accessing the forecasts and scores.
